abstract: |
  Solar and wind plants are cheap to build in most developing countries but expensive to finance, because lenders and investors price the risk that a state-owned distribution company will not pay for the power. This paper proposes a payment intermediary facility: a national or regional institution that buys power from generators under one standard contract, pays them in full and on time whatever the distributor does, and recovers arrears itself, behind a guarantee waterfall agreed in advance. I model offtaker default as recurring episodes of withheld payment with delayed, partial recovery. In a stylized calibration the offtaker premium adds 11 percent to the solar tariff, or 1.4 percentage points to the cost of capital. Guaranteeing the contract removes all of it and saves five dollars per dollar of the guarantor's expected cost; guaranteeing project debt saves less than it costs. India's Solar Energy Corporation shows that the design lowers tariffs, and its distributors' arrears show that it must be paired with utility reform. The state's exposure becomes smaller, contingent and contracted, but it does not vanish.

The views expressed are the author's own and do not represent those of any institution with which he is or has been affiliated. A short version is Climate Fiscal Policy Brief No. 2.1 [@CFPB21].*[^credits]

[^credits]: This paper consolidates and replaces earlier statements of the same architecture. The guarantee waterfall comes from a policy brief on regional renewable energy payment intermediary facilities written with Nils Zimmermann (2024). The treatment of small and debt-distressed states draws on the solar payments intermediary proposal developed by Evie Davey. Errors are mine.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Clean power in developing countries costs too much because its finance costs too much. A solar plant has no fuel bill, so the price of its electricity is mostly the repayment of the capital that built it. A stylized plant that needs 3.9 US cents per kilowatt-hour when financed at a 5 percent real cost of capital needs 6.5 cents at 12 percent. The International Energy Agency's surveys found that in 2021 the cost of capital for utility-scale solar in key emerging economies was two to three times that in advanced economies, and that financing made up about half of the levelized cost of solar in emerging and developing economies, against 25–30 percent in advanced economies and China [@IEA2022]. The agency estimates that cutting that gap by one percentage point would lower clean energy financing costs in these economies by about \$150 billion a year [@IEA2024].

A large part of the premium is the risk that the buyer of the power will not pay. In most developing countries that buyer, the offtaker, is a state-owned distribution company that sells below cost and collects poorly. Of 39 Sub-Saharan African countries studied by the World Bank, only Seychelles and Uganda had financially viable electricity sectors [@Trimble2016]. When such a utility runs short of cash, its generators wait. Lenders and investors price that wait into every project that sells to it, however good the project.

This paper asks how a developing country can remove the payment risk that sets the cost of capital for clean power, at the lowest contingent cost to the state.

The answer is to put a creditworthy intermediary between generators and distribution companies. A *payment intermediary facility* buys power from generators under one *standard power purchase agreement*, on-sells it to distribution companies, and pays generators in full and on time whatever the distribution companies do. It recovers arrears itself, and behind it stands a *guarantee waterfall*, contracted in advance: the offtaker, its subnational owner, the national government, a multilateral agency and a donor contingency account. Guaranteeing the contract beats guaranteeing project debt. It covers every project that sells to the same buyer, it keeps the claim on the distribution company alive, and it costs the guarantor the arrears it fails to recover rather than the face value of a loan. India's Solar Energy Corporation shows that the design can lower tariffs; its distribution companies' arrears show that it fails without utility reform.

The paper makes four contributions. First, it gives a tractable model of offtaker risk as recurring episodes of withheld payment with delayed, partial recovery, and derives the offtaker premium in the tariff (Proposition 1). The premium depends on how long arrears last and how much is recovered, which are exactly what an intermediary changes. Second, it states the conditions under which a contract guarantee dominates a debt guarantee in coverage, in the guarantor's expected cost and in tariff reduction per unit of expected cost (Proposition 2). The case for contract guarantees has been argued from practice [@StrettonTC]; this paper states its conditions. Third, it derives the expected calls on each layer of the waterfall and the liquidity buffer that makes the facility insolvency-remote under correlated offtaker defaults (Proposition 3). Fourth, it applies the results to verified public facts on India's Solar Energy Corporation and Nigeria's bulk electricity trader, and turns them into design rules on tariff profiles, currency, national versus regional facilities, countries in debt distress, utility reform and fiscal accounting. Relative to the de-risking literature, which classifies public instruments and estimates their effect on the cost of capital [@Waissbein2013; @Schmidt2014], the paper models a specific institution and compares two forms of guarantee. Relative to the literature on government guarantees [@Irwin2007; @PolackovaBrixi1998], it shows that one form of guarantee converts an implicit fiscal risk into a smaller, explicit and contracted one.

@sec-literature reviews the literature, @sec-model sets out the model, @sec-calibration calibrates it, @sec-precedents examines India and Nigeria, @sec-design turns to design, @sec-fiscal to fiscal accounting and @sec-policy to policy.

# Related literature {#sec-literature}

*The cost of capital decides the cost of renewables.* Because wind and solar are capital-intensive, their levelized cost is highly sensitive to the cost of capital. In Germany, improving financing conditions contributed substantially to the fall in the cost of renewable electricity [@Egli2018]. Estimates collected across many countries show that the cost of capital for renewable projects varies widely, and is generally higher in developing countries [@Steffen2020]. Higher finance costs in developing economies make low-carbon investment dearer relative to fossil investment and can lock them into a "climate investment trap" [@Ameli2021]. In integrated assessment models, letting developing-country costs of capital converge toward those of developed countries raises renewable deployment and lowers the cost of mitigation [@Calcaterra2024]. The IEA's Cost of Capital Observatory confirms the gap from survey data [@IEA2022; @IEA2024].

*De-risking.* A second literature asks how public instruments can lower these costs. The UN Development Programme's framework separates policy de-risking, which removes the source of a risk, from financial de-risking, which transfers it to a public actor, and estimates the effect of each on the levelized cost [@Waissbein2013]. Schmidt [-@Schmidt2014] argues that reducing investment risks can be cheaper for the public than compensating investors for bearing them. The payment intermediary sits across this divide. It transfers payment risk to a public institution, but because that institution is a repeat creditor with collection powers, it also lowers the risk, and the waterfall that backs it is conditional on reforms that remove the cause.

*Government guarantees and contingent liabilities.* Guarantees are options: a loan guarantee is a put on the borrower's assets with a strike equal to the debt [@Merton1977], and its cost to a government is the expected value of the calls it will meet, which governments often fail to budget [@Irwin2007]. Polackova [-@PolackovaBrixi1998] classifies government liabilities as direct or contingent, explicit or implicit; bailouts of state utilities are the textbook implicit contingent liability. Statistical standards record expected calls under schemes of many similar guarantees as a liability and disclose one-off guarantees as contingent [@IMF2014GFSM]. This paper uses these tools to compare the two forms of guarantee and to say how the facility's exposure should be recorded.

*Credit risk.* The model of offtaker default borrows from reduced-form credit models, in which defaults arrive at a random intensity and the value of a risky claim is found by discounting at a rate that adds the intensity times the loss on default [@DuffieSingleton1999]. Default risk is priced above its actuarial cost: bond prices imply default intensities above those observed, because default risk is partly undiversifiable [@Driessen2005]. For a portfolio of correlated offtakers, the one-factor model of Vasicek [-@Vasicek2002] gives the distribution of losses.

*The gap.* The literature establishes that the cost of capital matters and that de-risking lowers it, but it has not compared contract guarantees with debt guarantees formally, nor modeled an intermediary with a layered waterfall and its fiscal cost. Practitioner discussions describe payment security mechanisms [@ICRA2025], and earlier versions of this argument asserted the advantages of guaranteeing the offtaker rather than the loan [@StrettonTC]. This paper supplies the model, the conditions and a calibration.

# A model of offtaker risk and its guarantee {#sec-model}

## The cost of capital sets the tariff {#sec-lcoe}

A solar plant costs $I$ per kilowatt up front, costs $F$ per kilowatt a year to run, and produces $E$ kilowatt-hours per kilowatt a year for $T$ years. At a real weighted average cost of capital (WACC) $r$, its levelized cost is
$$
\mathrm{LCOE}(r) = \frac{I\,a(r) + F}{E}, \qquad a(r) = \frac{r}{1 - (1+r)^{-T}},
$$ {#eq-lcoe}
where $a(r)$ is the capital recovery factor. Since $F$ is small, the tariff rises almost in proportion to $a(r)$. The plant is the stylized plant used throughout this series: $I = \$800$, a 20 percent capacity factor ($E = 1{,}752$), $F = \$12$ and $T = 25$, with capital spent at commissioning. Paper 2.2 adds interest during a two-year construction period [@StrettonWP22].

## Offtaker default and the premium in the tariff {#sec-premium}

**Offtaker default.** The generator sells its output to one offtaker at a contracted tariff $P$ per kilowatt-hour, giving contracted payments of $A = PE$ a year. The offtaker falls into *default episodes*, which arrive at intensity $\lambda$ per year. In an episode the offtaker withholds all payments for $D$ years; at the end it pays a fraction $R$ of what it withheld, and the contract resumes. Episodes do not depend on the plant's own performance. Investors value the contract at the rate $r_0$, which prices every risk except the offtaker's, and they price episodes at a risk-neutral intensity $\lambda^Q = m\lambda$, with $m \ge 1$ the market price of default risk.

Two quantities summarize the process. The share of time the offtaker spends in arrears is
$$
\varphi(\lambda) = \frac{\lambda D}{1 + \lambda D},
$$ {#eq-phi}
and a payment withheld at a random point of an episode and paid at its end is worth, at the start of the episode,
$$
\tilde R = R\,\frac{1 - e^{-r_0 D}}{r_0 D}
$$ {#eq-rtilde}
of its face value. The generator therefore expects to receive a fraction $1 - h$ of every contracted dollar, where the *offtaker haircut* is
$$
h = \varphi(m\lambda)\,(1 - \tilde R).
$$ {#eq-haircut}

**Proposition 1 (offtaker premium).** *In the stationary regime, the break-even tariff for a generator exposed to the offtaker is*
$$
P^{*} = \frac{\mathrm{LCOE}(r_0)}{1 - h},
$$ {#eq-premium}
*so the offtaker premium in the tariff is $\mathrm{LCOE}(r_0)\,h/(1-h)$. It rises with the frequency $\lambda$ and length $D$ of episodes and with the price of risk $m$, and falls with the recovery rate $R$. It is equivalent to raising the WACC to $r^{*}$, where $\mathrm{LCOE}(r^{*}) = P^{*}$.*

The proof is in @sec-appA. The intuition is that a generator who expects to collect 90 cents of each contracted dollar must charge 11 percent more. Two features matter for policy. First, frequent short delays cost little if they are fully recovered: the haircut depends on $1 - \tilde R$, so an offtaker that is often late but always pays in the end carries a small premium. What investors charge for is long arrears and losses on recovery. Second, every term in $h$ is something an intermediary can change. A facility with liquidity shortens the episode the generator experiences to zero; a facility with powers to intercept transfers raises $R$; and a facility that is a repeat creditor of the offtaker lowers $\lambda$ itself, because the offtaker cannot play one generator off against another.

## Guarantee the contract or guarantee the debt {#sec-guarantees}

A public guarantor can cover the generator's contract or the project's debt. Under a *contract guarantee* the guarantor (here, the facility) pays the generator the contracted amount during every episode, and recovers from the offtaker a fraction $R_G$ of what it paid, $D_G$ years after the episode ends. Under a *debt guarantee* the guarantor pays the project's lenders when the project fails to service its debt, from any cause, and recovers a fraction $R_D$ by subrogation against the project company, $D_D$ years later. Let $g$ be the share of capital financed by debt.

The two guarantees remove different parts of the risk. A contract guarantee removes the whole haircut $h$, because the generator is paid in full. A debt guarantee removes only the part that would fall on lenders. Write that part as $\theta h$, with $0 \le \theta \le 1$. When the equity cushion and debt service reserve absorb every episode, $\theta = 0$: the lenders were never at risk, and the guarantee removes nothing from the tariff. $\theta$ rises with leverage and with the length of episodes. A debt guarantee also covers non-payment from other causes, such as construction failure or plant breakdown, whose expected cost to the guarantor I write as $\psi \ge 0$ per unit of contracted payments.

Let the facility's recovery value be $\tilde R_G = R_G\,\frac{1 - e^{-r_0 D}}{r_0 D}\,e^{-r_0 D_G}$ and the debt guarantor's be $\tilde R_D = R_D\,e^{-r_0 D_D}$.

**Proposition 2 (contract versus debt guarantee).** *Under the assumptions of Proposition 1:*

*(i) Coverage. The tariff under a contract guarantee is $P_C = \mathrm{LCOE}(r_0)$; under a debt guarantee it is $P_D = \mathrm{LCOE}(r_0)/(1 - (1-\theta)h) \ge P_C$, with equality only if all offtaker losses fall on lenders ($\theta = 1$). One contract guarantee covers every project selling to the guaranteed offtaker.*

*(ii) Expected cost. Per unit of contracted payments, the contract guarantor's expected annual cost is $c_C = \varphi(\lambda)(1 - \tilde R_G)$, and its exposure in any one episode is bounded by the arrears $AD$. The debt guarantor's expected cost is $c_D = \theta\varphi(\lambda)(1 - \tilde R_D) + \psi$, and its exposure is bounded only by the outstanding debt.*

*(iii) Efficiency. The offtaker loss removed per unit of the guarantor's expected cost is*
$$
\frac{h}{c_C} = \frac{\varphi(m\lambda)}{\varphi(\lambda)}\cdot\frac{1 - \tilde R}{1 - \tilde R_G}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\frac{\theta h}{c_D} = \frac{\theta h}{\theta\varphi(\lambda)(1 - \tilde R_D) + \psi}.
$$ {#eq-efficiency}
*The contract guarantee is at least as efficient whenever $\tilde R_G \ge \tilde R_D$, that is, whenever the contract guarantor recovers at least as much, in present value, as a debt guarantor would. It removes more value than it costs in expectation whenever $m \ge 1$ and $\tilde R_G \ge \tilde R$.*

The conditions are the substance of the result. The recovery condition $\tilde R_G \ge \tilde R_D$ holds whenever the contract guarantor keeps a claim on the offtaker and the debt guarantor's claim runs against a project company whose only asset is an unpaid contract. It fails if the facility cannot enforce its claim, which is why the waterfall matters. The efficiency ratio in @eq-efficiency splits into two parts with different welfare meanings. The second factor, $(1-\tilde R)/(1-\tilde R_G)$, is a real resource gain: the facility recovers more than a dispersed set of generators would, because it is a repeat creditor with collection powers. The first factor, $\varphi(m\lambda)/\varphi(\lambda)$, is the market price of risk that investors no longer charge. That part is a gain to society only if the state is better placed to bear the risk than investors are. It is not when the offtaker's default is correlated with the state's own fiscal distress, as it often is, and @sec-fiscal returns to that point.

A debt guarantee is not always worse. Where there is no contract to guarantee, as for transmission lines or factories, a guarantee on the bond is the only option, and the series treats it in Paper 2.2 [@CFPB22]. Where the offtaker is sound and the main risk is construction, a guarantee targeted on construction finance is better than either. The proposition says that where offtaker payment is the binding risk, the guarantee should attach to the payment.

## The facility under a guarantee waterfall {#sec-waterfall}

The facility holds a portfolio of contracts with $M$ offtakers, paying $A$ a year in total. Behind the offtakers stand layers $k = 1, \dots, K$: the subnational owner, the national government, a multilateral agency and a donor contingency account. When an episode leaves arrears unrecovered, the shortfall passes down the layers in order; layer $k$ pays in full with probability $q_k$, independently of the layers above it, and otherwise passes the shortfall on. The facility holds a liquidity buffer $B$ to pay generators while it waits for a layer to pay, which takes up to $H$ years. Episodes across offtakers are correlated through a common factor: each offtaker enters an episode within a year with probability $p = 1 - e^{-\lambda}$, and the latent variables driving episodes have pairwise correlation $\rho$.

**Proposition 3 (expected calls and insolvency remoteness).** *(i) The expected annual call on layer $k$ is*
$$
C_k = \varphi(\lambda)\,A\,(1 - \tilde R)\; q_k \prod_{j<k}(1 - q_j),
$$ {#eq-calls}
*and the facility's own expected loss is $\varphi(\lambda)A(1 - \tilde R)\prod_{k=1}^{K}(1 - q_k)$, which is zero if the last layer is funded and certain ($q_K = 1$).*

*(ii) In a large portfolio, the facility can pay generators in full at confidence $1 - \varepsilon$ if*
$$
B \ \ge\ A\,H\,\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(p) + \sqrt{\rho}\,\Phi^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)
$$ {#eq-buffer}
*and the last layer's committed capacity covers the shortfall that reaches it at the same confidence. Under these conditions the facility is insolvency-remote: every loss is borne by a contracted layer, never by generators.*

Part (i) shows where the cost of the guarantee falls. Each layer's expected cost depends on the reliability of the layers above it, so a reliable intercept by the national government ($q_2$ near one) makes the multilateral and donor layers cheap. Part (ii) is the standard large-portfolio result [@Vasicek2002] applied to arrears rather than losses. It shows why diversification has limits: when offtaker defaults are driven by a common shock, such as a devaluation or a fuel price spike, the buffer must be sized for the share of offtakers in arrears at the same time, not for the average. The calls $C_k$ are expected payments, not final losses. A national government that pays a utility's arrears acquires a claim on its own utility; whether it collects is a question of utility reform, not of the facility's design.

# Calibration {#sec-calibration}

## The plant and the price of capital {#sec-cal-plant}

The stylized 100-megawatt plant costs \$80 million and produces 175,200 megawatt-hours a year. @tbl-lcoe and @fig-lcoe show its levelized cost at real WACCs from 4 to 15 percent. Moving from 12 percent to 5 percent cuts the tariff from 6.5 to 3.9 cents per kilowatt-hour, and the annual revenue the plant needs from \$11.4 million to \$6.9 million. At 8 percent each percentage point of WACC is worth 0.37 cents per kilowatt-hour, about 7 percent of the tariff. The return on capital, the part of the tariff above straight-line depreciation and operating costs, rises from 30 percent of the tariff at 4 percent to 61 percent at 12 percent, consistent with the IEA's finding that financing is about half the cost of solar in emerging and developing economies [@IEA2022].

| WACC (real) | 4% | 5% | 6% | 8% | 10% | 12% | 15% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Levelized cost (US cents/kWh) | 3.61 | 3.92 | 4.26 | 4.96 | 5.72 | 6.51 | 7.75 |
| Relative to 4% | 1.00 | 1.09 | 1.18 | 1.38 | 1.58 | 1.80 | 2.15 |
| Return on capital, share of cost | 30% | 36% | 41% | 49% | 56% | 61% | 68% |

: The same solar plant costs twice as much at 15 percent as at 4 percent (stylized plant: \$800/kW, 20 percent capacity factor, \$12/kW-year operation and maintenance, 25 years, capital spent at commissioning with no interest during construction). Paper 2.2 adds a two-year construction period at the financing rate, which raises the cost at 10 percent from 5.72 to 6.22 cents [@StrettonWP22]. Source: `2.Source/model.py`. {#tbl-lcoe}

![Levelized cost of the stylized solar plant by real WACC. The shaded band is the offtaker premium of the central case in @tbl-premium, added to an 8 percent WACC that prices every other risk. Source: `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig1_lcoe_wacc.png){#fig-lcoe width=90%}

## How much the offtaker costs {#sec-cal-premium}

The central case assumes a WACC of 8 percent for every risk except the offtaker's, one default episode every six to seven years ($\lambda = 0.15$), episodes lasting a year ($D = 1$), recovery of 60 percent of withheld payments ($R = 0.6$), and a price of risk $m = 2$. All five are stylized. They describe a weak but not failed utility, one that is regularly late and eventually pays most of what it owes. The value of $m$ reflects the finding that bond prices imply default intensities above observed ones [@Driessen2005]; I do not claim a point estimate.

In the central case the offtaker is in arrears 23 percent of the time at the risk-neutral intensity, a withheld dollar is worth 58 cents in present value, and the haircut $h$ is 9.8 percent. The break-even tariff rises from 4.96 to 5.50 cents per kilowatt-hour, an offtaker premium of 0.54 cents or 10.8 percent, equivalent to a WACC of 9.4 percent instead of 8. @tbl-premium and @fig-premium show how the premium varies. A utility with 25 episodes per 100 years that pays back only 30 percent of what it withholds adds 4 percentage points to the WACC; one that is late as often but pays back 90 percent adds 0.6 points. Episodes of six months halve the central-case premium, and episodes of two years nearly double it. Without a price of risk ($m = 1$) the premium falls to 5.8 percent of the tariff.

| Episodes per 100 offtaker-years | Recovery 30% | Recovery 60% | Recovery 90% |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 5 | 6.9% (+0.9) | 4.0% (+0.5) | 1.2% (+0.2) |
| 10 | 13.5% (+1.8) | 7.6% (+1.0) | 2.3% (+0.3) |
| 15 | 19.7% (+2.6) | **10.8% (+1.4)** | 3.2% (+0.4) |
| 25 | 31.1% (+4.0) | 16.4% (+2.2) | 4.7% (+0.6) |

: Recovery matters as much as frequency: offtaker premium as a share of the tariff, with the equivalent rise in WACC in percentage points in brackets (stylized). Episodes last one year; price of risk $m = 2$; base WACC 8 percent. The central case is in bold. Source: `2.Source/model.py`. {#tbl-premium}

![Offtaker premium in the WACC by frequency of default episodes and share of withheld payments eventually recovered (stylized; one-year episodes, $m = 2$, base WACC 8 percent). Source: `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig2_offtaker_premium.png){#fig-premium width=90%}

These magnitudes are plausible against observed gaps. The IEA puts the cost of capital for solar in emerging economies at two to three times that of advanced economies [@IEA2022], a gap of several percentage points, of which the offtaker is one part alongside sovereign, currency and other risks. The central case attributes 1.4 points to the offtaker. I treat this as an illustration of mechanism, not an estimate.

## Contract versus debt guarantee in numbers {#sec-cal-guarantee}

@tbl-guarantee applies Proposition 2 to the 100-megawatt plant. The facility recovers 95 percent of what it pays, a year after each episode ends, because it can call on the waterfall; the debt guarantor recovers 50 percent, three years later, from the project company. Debt is 75 percent of capital, so the plant borrows \$60 million. Lenders bear 30 percent of the offtaker's losses ($\theta = 0.3$), and the debt guarantee also covers other risks with an expected cost of 1 percent a year of a 30 percent loss on the debt. All of these are stylized.

| Stylized 100 MW solar plant | No guarantee | Contract guarantee | Debt guarantee |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Tariff (US cents/kWh) | 5.50 | 4.96 | 5.33 |
| Saving to the offtaker (\$ million/year) | – | 0.94 | 0.30 |
| Guarantor's expected cost (\$ million/year) | – | 0.18 | 0.40 |
| of which offtaker-driven | – | 0.18 | 0.22 |
| of which other risks | – | 0 | 0.18 |
| Saving per dollar of expected cost | – | 5.3 | 0.8 |
| Maximum exposure (\$ million) | – | 8.7 per year of arrears | 60 of debt at close |

: A contract guarantee buys more tariff reduction for less risk (stylized). Parameters in the text and @sec-appB. Source: `2.Source/model.py`. {#tbl-guarantee}

The contract guarantee cuts the tariff by 0.54 cents, the whole offtaker premium, and saves the offtaker \$0.94 million a year; the facility's expected cost is \$0.18 million. The debt guarantee cuts the tariff by 0.17 cents and costs its guarantor \$0.40 million a year, nearly half of it for risks unrelated to the offtaker. Per dollar of expected cost, the contract guarantee saves \$5.3 and the debt guarantee \$0.8 (@fig-guarantee). The efficiency ratio of Proposition 2(iii), 4.8 in value terms, splits into a factor of 1.8 from the price of risk and 2.7 from the facility's better recovery. Even with no price of risk, the contract guarantee would remove nearly three times its expected cost.

![Saving to the offtaker and expected cost to the guarantor, contract versus debt guarantee, stylized 100 MW plant. Source: `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig3_contract_vs_debt.png){#fig-guarantee width=90%}

The exposures differ by an order of magnitude. The facility's worst case in one episode is a year of unpaid bills, \$8.7 million, most of which it recovers. The debt guarantor's worst case is the loan, \$60 million at financial close. That difference is the difference between a guarantee priced at expected loss and one that must be capitalized at face value.

## A regional facility under its waterfall {#sec-cal-waterfall}

Consider a regional facility that buys the output of 2 gigawatts of solar plants from ten offtakers, under the central-case parameters, with contract payments of \$174 million a year. The facility expects to fund \$22.7 million of arrears a year, of which 42 percent in present value is not recovered from the offtakers themselves. @tbl-waterfall and @fig-waterfall show where that shortfall goes, with stylized probabilities that each layer pays: the subnational owner 0.5, the national government 0.8, a multilateral agency 0.9 and a funded donor account 1.

| Layer | Probability it pays when called | Expected call (\$ million/year) | Share of contract payments |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Subnational owner | 0.5 | 4.80 | 2.76% |
| National government | 0.8 | 3.84 | 2.21% |
| Multilateral agency | 0.9 | 0.86 | 0.50% |
| Donor contingency account | 1.0 | 0.10 | 0.06% |
| Facility (residual) | – | 0 | 0 |

: Most of the cost falls on the offtaker's owners, little on donors (stylized regional facility, 2 GW, contract payments \$174 million a year). Expected calls are payments, not final losses: the subnational and national layers acquire claims on their own utilities. Source: `2.Source/model.py`. {#tbl-waterfall}

![Expected annual value recovered from offtakers and expected calls on each layer of the waterfall, stylized 2 GW regional facility. Source: `2.Source/make_wp_figures.py`.](2.Source/figures/fig4_waterfall.png){#fig-waterfall width=90%}

Three results follow. The donor account at the bottom is cheap, \$0.1 million a year, because the national layer is reliable; if the national government's intercept worked only half the time, the donor's expected cost would rise two and a half times. The facility's own expected loss is zero with the donor account and 0.06 percent of payments without it, well within a trading margin like India's. And the expected calls on the subnational and national layers, about 5 percent of payments, are the price of the offtakers' unreliability, paid by their owners rather than by consumers through a risk premium on every project.

Liquidity, not loss, is what can break the facility. If episodes are driven by a common factor with correlation 0.3, the share of offtakers in arrears in a 1-in-200 year is 65 percent, against an average of 14 percent. A facility that must wait six months for the national layer then needs a buffer of \$57 million, a third of a year's payments or about \$28,000 per megawatt (@eq-buffer). With correlation 0.1 the stress share falls to 39 percent; with 0.5 it rises to 85 percent. For comparison, India's Solar Energy Corporation asks developers in newer tenders to deposit Rs 5 lakh per megawatt toward its payment security fund [@ICRA2025], about \$6,000 at roughly Rs 85 per dollar; it relies on letters of credit and the intercept for the rest.

## India in the model {#sec-cal-india}

The Solar Energy Corporation of India earns a trading margin of Rs 0.07 per kilowatt-hour on a weighted average sale tariff of Rs 2.93 [@ICRA2025], or 2.4 percent of the tariff. In the model the margin pays for itself if the intermediary lowers the WACC by 0.35 percentage points, a quarter of the central-case offtaker premium. Applied to the corporation's roughly 60 gigawatts of sale agreements, at the stylized plant's capacity factor, the central-case premium would cost about Rs 3,300 crore a year, against a margin of about Rs 740 crore. These numbers are illustrative: wind contracts have different capacity factors, and the counterfactual premium for Indian state distribution companies is not observed. A direct comparison of tariffs in the corporation's auctions with those in auctions run by state distribution companies on their own credit would test Proposition 1. I have not found public data clean enough to do it here.

# Precedents and failures {#sec-precedents}

## India's Solar Energy Corporation: the waterfall works, the buyers were not fixed {#sec-seci}

The Solar Energy Corporation of India is the clearest working example of a payment intermediary facility. It is wholly owned by the central government and administered by the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy. It signs power purchase agreements with developers only after it has signed back-to-back power sale agreements with state distribution companies on similar terms, so it carries no demand risk. In July 2025 it had sale agreements for about 60 gigawatts at a weighted average tariff of Rs 2.93 per kilowatt-hour, which the rating agency ICRA describes as well below the distribution companies' average power purchase cost [@ICRA2025].

Its payment security is layered, much as @sec-waterfall proposes. Each layer can be checked against public sources:

* *Letters of credit.* Distribution companies must open letters of credit for the corporation, which earns its Rs 0.07 margin subject to their opening [@ICRA2025]. A Ministry of Power order of 28 June 2019, effective 1 August 2019, made letters of credit mandatory under power purchase agreements and instructed load dispatch centers to schedule power only once they were in place [@Powerline2019].
* *Payment security fund.* A fund financed from central budgetary support, penalties recovered from developers and interest covers capacity awarded under batches I, III and IV of phase II of the National Solar Mission. Since amendments to the bidding guidelines in October 2019, developers in later tenders deposit Rs 5 lakh per megawatt toward it. The fund does not yet cover other schemes [@ICRA2025].
* *Tripartite agreement.* Since October 2016 the corporation has been a beneficiary of the tripartite agreement among the central government, the state governments and the Reserve Bank of India [@ICRA2025; @Kenning2017]. Under it, a central utility owed money can ask the central government to instruct the Reserve Bank to debit the defaulting state's account and credit the utility. All but two states and union territories have signed it. The corporation invoked it in fiscal years 2021 and 2022 against distribution companies in Andhra Pradesh and against HESCOM in Karnataka [@ICRA2025].
* *Sovereign support.* The central government injected Rs 1,000 crore of equity in March 2022 [@ICRA2025].

Older drafts of this paper said the corporation draws on credit lines with the Reserve Bank of India. The public record does not support that. The Reserve Bank's role is that of a debiting agent under the tripartite agreement, which works through the state's own account rather than through central bank credit.

The design has done what Proposition 2 predicts. ICRA rates the corporation AAA, citing its sovereign parentage, the tripartite agreement and its collection record [@ICRA2025]. The agreement's value lies as much in deterrence as in use: a state that defaults on the corporation loses central transfers, so the corporation is paid ahead of generators that sell to the state directly.

The failure is upstream. The same rating report notes that most state distribution companies remain financially weak, with losses above approved levels and tariffs below cost, that delays from Andhra Pradesh and Karnataka were once large, and that distribution companies' letter-of-credit coverage is only 68 percent [@ICRA2025]. Across the sector the central government has had to act twice. In May 2020 it announced a Rs 90,000 crore liquidity scheme, under which two public finance companies lent to distribution companies against state guarantees so that they could pay generators [@CRISIL2020]. In June 2022 the Electricity (Late Payment Surcharge and Related Matters) Rules let distribution companies pay their accumulated arrears in up to 48 monthly installments, with surcharges waived on timely payment [@Powerline2022]. Legacy arrears under the rules fell from Rs 1,39,947 crore on 3 June 2022 to Rs 3,330 crore on 27 March 2026, according to a written reply in Parliament [@PTI2026].

India's record therefore confirms both halves of the argument. The intermediary and its waterfall moved the risk away from generators and lowered tariffs. But the risk moved to the central government; it was not removed. The center paid for liquidity in 2020 and restructured arrears in 2022, and in both cases it recovered most of its money because it could reach the states. That is the waterfall working as Proposition 3 describes, with the national layer paying when called and recovering over time. It is also a warning that a waterfall without utility reform turns into a standing line of credit.

## Nigeria's bulk trader: a single buyer with nothing behind it {#sec-nbet}

Nigeria created the Nigerian Bulk Electricity Trading company (NBET) under its 2010 power sector roadmap as a single buyer that purchases power from generators and on-sells it to distribution companies [@WBGAzura]. In form it is a payment intermediary. In substance it lacked the two things that make one work: revenue from its buyers and a contracted layer behind it.

The revenue never arrived. In 2017 the government arranged a central bank loan of up to N701 billion through the Ministry of Finance, repayable by the trader over ten years, so that it could pay generators and gas suppliers; at the time the trader expected to collect on average about a quarter of its invoices from the distribution companies [@Okafor2017]. In June 2020 the World Bank approved a \$750 million credit for Nigeria's power sector recovery program, aimed among other things at reducing the sector's annual tariff shortfalls [@WorldBank2020PSRO]. An intermediary that collects a quarter of its bills is a conduit for subsidy, not a credit enhancement.

The country's first project-financed independent power plant shows what happens when guarantees attach to debt instead. For the 459-megawatt Azura-Edo gas plant, which reached financial close in December 2015, the World Bank Group provided guarantees of \$238 million: a payment guarantee of up to \$120 million backing the trader's payment security obligations, and a guarantee of up to \$118 million that allowed a commercial debt tranche, alongside political risk cover from the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency [@WBGAzura]. Because the government would not give a sovereign guarantee, it signed a put-and-call option agreement instead. If the power purchase agreement ends early, the project company can put the plant to the government, which must pay a price that at a minimum covers the outstanding debt. The World Bank Group's case study describes this as support "with no negative impact on FGN's balance sheet" [@WBGAzura].

That description shows exactly the accounting problem @sec-fiscal addresses. The payment guarantee is a contract guarantee in the sense of this paper, capped and tied to the trader's obligations. The put option is a debt guarantee with a delay: its trigger is the failure of the contract, and its payout is the face value of the debt. In the terms of Proposition 2, it has the large maximum exposure of a debt guarantee and none of the recovery of a contract guarantee, since once the government owns the plant there is no one left to recover from. It is a contingent liability of the state and should be recorded as one.

# Design {#sec-design}

## Tariff profile: declining, not flat {#sec-tariff}

A flat real tariff for 20 years locks the offtaker into the price of the year the contract was signed. If the cost of new solar halves, the offtaker pays double the going rate for the rest of the contract, and its government comes under pressure to renegotiate. Renegotiation is itself a form of default, so a flat tariff raises $\lambda$.

A declining tariff reduces the exposure without changing the present value. At an 8 percent discount rate, a tariff that starts at 7.74 cents and falls in a straight line to 3.87 cents by year 7, then stays flat, has the same present value over 20 years as a flat 5 cents (stylized). By year 7 the value of the payments still due is 23 percent lower under the declining tariff, 30.6 against 39.5 cent-kilowatt-hour-years. If the cost of new solar falls from 5 to 2.5 cents over the same seven years, the part of the remaining payments above new-build cost is 45 percent lower, 10.8 against 19.8. Earlier drafts proposed a tariff of 6 cents falling to 3 cents as equivalent in present value to a flat 5 cents; at 8 percent it is worth 22 percent less, so developers would not accept it.

The declining tariff therefore saves nothing in present value. What it buys is a contract that stays close to the market price and so is less tempting to break, and a smaller outstanding obligation for the guarantor in later years. The cost is a higher starting tariff, which falls on the offtaker when solar is still a small share of its purchases. The facility should index the decline to a conservative published path rather than to forecasts of technology costs.

## One currency rule {#sec-currency}

*Contract in the currency the offtaker earns.* A distribution company earns local currency. A tariff in dollars hands it, and behind it the state, the devaluation risk of every contract, and that risk arrives when the state can least bear it, in a balance of payments crisis. In the model it makes $\lambda$ and the offtakers' correlation $\rho$ rise together, which is the worst case for the buffer in @eq-buffer.

Where projects are financed in foreign currency, the facility, not the offtaker, should decide how the mismatch is held, and it should be priced in the open. It can buy hedges from specialist providers such as the Currency Exchange Fund (TCX) where they exist; index only the share of the tariff that pays for imported equipment, for a limited period; or fund the contracts from domestic savings, which removes the mismatch at source. Paper 2.2 sets out a local-currency senior tranche for domestic savers [@CFPB22]. The rule excludes one practice: a hard-currency tariff whose currency risk is never priced because the state's guarantee hides it.

## National or regional {#sec-regional}

Large markets should build national facilities. India, Nigeria and Brazil each have enough distribution companies, and enough procurement, to diversify across offtakers and to justify a specialist institution. A national facility can rely on a domestic intercept like India's tripartite agreement, which gives the national layer a high probability of paying.

Small states should share a regional facility. A facility serving, for example, the members of the Economic Community of West African States would spread the fixed costs of standard contracts, procurement and collection across many projects, and diversify across offtakers whose utilities fail for different reasons. But a regional facility has a weaker national layer. No regional facility has an intercept as direct as India's, so $q_2$ is lower and the multilateral and donor layers bear more (@eq-calls). Members can strengthen it by depositing letters of credit or reserves with the facility, by agreeing to offset arrears against transfers they receive from regional institutions, and by giving the facility's claims the same seniority as their obligations to multilateral lenders.

## Countries in debt distress: energy as a service {#sec-eaas}

A country that cannot borrow more can still buy clean power. The facility, or a private developer under its standard contract, owns and finances the plant, and the state's utility buys the electricity per kilowatt-hour. The state replaces an open-ended, foreign-currency fuel bill with a fixed and, under a declining tariff, falling local-currency one.

This changes the form of the state's obligation, not its existence. A long-term take-or-pay power purchase agreement is a fiscal commitment, and a guarantee behind it is a contingent liability. Earlier versions of this proposal described the arrangement as outside the debt stock and protected by the World Bank Group's preferred creditor status; neither claim survives scrutiny, and this paper drops both. The defensible claim is narrower: the commitment is smaller than the fuel bill it replaces, its terms are fixed and known, and it falls due only if the state's own utility fails to pay. Debt sustainability analysis should count it, and should also count the fuel import bill it removes.

## Conditionality on utility reform {#sec-reform}

A guarantee makes the generator whole; it does not make the utility solvent. India's arrears show what happens when the waterfall is not matched by reform: the national layer pays repeatedly, and a contingent liability becomes a recurrent one. A country that will not put its utility on a path to cost recovery is asking the guarantor to insure a certain loss rather than a risk.

Entry to the facility should therefore be conditional, and access should widen as the conditions are met. The conditions follow from the model. A published path of tariffs toward cost recovery, and an explicit budget transfer for any subsidy that remains, lower the frequency of episodes $\lambda$. Letters of credit and an intercept agreement raise the recovery $R$ and the national layer's probability $q_2$. Targets for collection and loss reduction lower $\lambda$ over time. Because cheap solar lowers the utility's cost of supply, reform and the facility reinforce each other: the facility makes the tariff path shorter, and the tariff path makes the facility cheaper. Sustainability-linked sovereign lending, discussed in Paper 3.3 [@CFPB33], is one way to pay for the reforms.

# Fiscal accounting of the contingent liability {#sec-fiscal}

The facility does not make the state's exposure disappear. It changes its form in three ways: it becomes smaller, because the facility recovers more than generators would and because reform conditions lower the frequency of default; it becomes contingent, because the state pays only when its own utility fails to; and it becomes contracted, because the waterfall fixes in advance who pays, in what order and up to what cap.

The comparison that matters is with what the state already holds. Before the facility, the state bears its utilities' arrears implicitly. India's liquidity scheme of 2020 and its rescheduling of arrears in 2022, and Nigeria's central bank facility of 2017, are implicit contingent liabilities falling due, in the classification of Polackova [-@PolackovaBrixi1998]. The facility converts part of this implicit liability into an explicit one with a cap and a price. The state's total exposure to its utilities need not rise, and the reform conditions should make it fall.

The facility's layers should be recorded at their expected cost. The IMF's Government Finance Statistics Manual records, as a liability, provisions for the expected calls under standardized guarantee schemes, where many similar guarantees are issued on the same terms, while one-off guarantees are disclosed as contingent liabilities until called [@IMF2014GFSM]. A facility with one standard power purchase agreement and many offtakers is a standardized scheme. The national government should therefore record a provision equal to its expected calls net of expected recovery, $C_2$ in @eq-calls less what it expects to recover from its utility, and disclose the stressed call at a stated confidence level. In the stylized regional facility of @tbl-waterfall, the national layer's expected call is 2.2 percent of contract payments a year, before recovery.

The guarantee should also be capped in law and charged for. A cap, set as a multiple of annual contract payments, limits the tail that @eq-buffer leaves to the national layer. A fee charged to the facility, and passed to the utilities that cause the calls, makes the cost visible, as @Irwin2007 recommends for infrastructure guarantees generally. Terminations and buy-out options such as Nigeria's put-and-call agreement belong in the same register at their full contingent value, not outside it.

The model's efficiency ratio carries a fiscal caveat. Part of the gain in @eq-efficiency comes from the market price of risk, which investors stop charging once the state bears the risk. That part is a saving to society only if the state bears the risk more cheaply than investors. When the utility's default is correlated with the state's own fiscal stress, as in a currency crisis, the state is a poor holder of that risk, and the multilateral and donor layers earn their place by holding the correlated tail.

# Policy implications {#sec-policy}

*What to build.* Governments whose distribution companies buy most of the power should create, or join, a payment intermediary facility with one standard power purchase agreement and a guarantee waterfall signed before the first tender. Large countries should build national facilities; small countries should share regional ones with a stronger multilateral layer. New utility-scale renewable procurement should run through the facility, in local currency and on declining tariffs.

*What it costs.* In the stylized calibration the facility needs a margin of a few percent of contract payments, like India's 2.4 percent, and a liquidity buffer of about a third of a year's payments. The layers behind it expect to be called for about 5 percent of payments a year, mostly by the offtakers' own owners and mostly recoverable. Against this, the contract guarantee removes an offtaker premium worth about 11 percent of the tariff in the central case.

*Who should do what.* Finance ministries should sign the intercept, set the reform conditions and record their layer at expected cost under a published cap. Regulators should require letters of credit and enforce dispatch rules like India's. Development banks should guarantee the facility, or stand as its multilateral layer, rather than guaranteeing individual project loans. Donors should fund the contingency account at the bottom of the waterfall. Once the contracts are standard and guaranteed, the plants they support can be refinanced as a few homogeneous asset classes through two-stage finance and synthetic sovereign bonds [@CFPB22; @StrettonWP22], with first-loss capital from the regional funds of a Climate Investment Trust [@CFPB32].

*When it fails.* The recommendation fails under four conditions. If utility losses are structural and reform does not come, the waterfall becomes a channel for a permanent subsidy, and the honest instrument is an explicit budget transfer. If the national layer cannot or will not pay, as in a regional facility without an intercept, the cost shifts to multilateral and donor layers that may not be willing to bear it. If a common shock drives most offtakers into arrears together, the buffer in @eq-buffer must be large, and an underfunded facility fails exactly when it is needed. And if the facility is captured, signing contracts above cost for favored developers, it spreads the cost of bad contracts across the whole system. Governance should therefore separate procurement, which sets prices by open auction, from payment, which the facility runs to fixed rules.

*The strongest objection* is that the facility only moves risk to the center, as India shows. That is true and is the point. The center already holds the risk implicitly and pays it in crises, as India did in 2020 and 2022 and Nigeria in 2017. The facility makes the center's exposure smaller, by raising recovery and lowering the frequency of default through conditions; contingent, by placing it behind the utility and its owner; and contracted, by fixing its order and cap in advance. The alternative is to pay the offtaker premium on every project, every year, for the life of every contract.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

The payment risk of a state utility is the part of the cost of clean power that a developing country can most easily remove. A payment intermediary facility removes it at source by guaranteeing the contract rather than the debt. The model in this paper shows that the offtaker premium depends on the length of arrears and on recovery, both of which an intermediary can change; that a contract guarantee removes the whole premium at a fraction of its value when the guarantor keeps an enforceable claim on the offtaker; and that a layered waterfall puts the expected cost on the offtakers' owners and keeps the facility insolvency-remote if it holds enough liquidity for correlated arrears. India's Solar Energy Corporation confirms the mechanism and its limit: generators were paid, but the center had to fund the distribution companies twice.

The main limitation is that the calibration is stylized. The next step is empirical: estimating the frequency, length and recovery of default episodes for named utilities from payment data such as India's PRAAPTI portal, and comparing tariffs in intermediated and direct auctions to measure the offtaker premium that Proposition 1 describes.

# Appendix A: Proofs {.appendix .unnumbered #sec-appA}

*Proposition 1.* Model the offtaker as an alternating renewal process: normal periods with exponential length of mean $1/\lambda^Q$ under the pricing measure, and episodes of fixed length $D$. By the renewal–reward theorem the long-run share of time in an episode is $D/(1/\lambda^Q + D) = \varphi(\lambda^Q)$. A payment due at time $s \in [0, D]$ after the start of an episode is paid, in fraction $R$, at time $D$; its value at the time it fell due is $Re^{-r_0(D-s)}$. Averaging over $s$ uniformly on $[0, D]$ gives $R(1 - e^{-r_0 D})/(r_0 D) = \tilde R$. In the stationary regime, therefore, each contracted dollar is worth $(1 - \varphi) + \varphi\tilde R = 1 - h$ in expectation under the pricing measure, where $h = \varphi(\lambda^Q)(1 - \tilde R)$. The generator breaks even when the value of contracted payments, $(1-h)PE/a(r_0)$, equals the value of costs, $I + F/a(r_0)$; solving gives $P^{*} = \mathrm{LCOE}(r_0)/(1-h)$. The comparative statics follow because $\varphi$ is increasing in $\lambda^Q = m\lambda$ and in $D$, $\tilde R$ is increasing in $R$ and decreasing in $D$, and $h/(1-h)$ is increasing in $h$. Since $\mathrm{LCOE}(r)$ is continuous and strictly increasing in $r$, a unique $r^{*}$ solves $\mathrm{LCOE}(r^{*}) = P^{*}$. The approximation $r^{*} - r_0 \approx \mathrm{LCOE}(r_0)\,h/[(1-h)\,\mathrm{LCOE}'(r_0)]$ holds for small $h$.

*Proposition 2.* (i) Under a contract guarantee the generator receives every contracted dollar, so $h$ is replaced by zero in Proposition 1. Under a debt guarantee the share $\theta$ of the haircut that would have fallen on lenders is borne by the guarantor, so the project's haircut is $(1-\theta)h$; since $1/(1-x)$ is increasing, $P_D \ge P_C$ with equality iff $(1-\theta)h = 0$. The contract guarantee attaches to the offtaker's obligation, which is identical across the standard contracts it has signed, so a single guarantee covers all of them. (ii) Under the physical measure the facility funds a share $\varphi(\lambda)$ of contracted payments and recovers, in present value at the time each payment fell due, $R_G(1 - e^{-r_0 D})/(r_0 D)e^{-r_0 D_G} = \tilde R_G$, giving $c_C = \varphi(\lambda)(1 - \tilde R_G)$. In any episode it pays at most the payments due during the episode, $AD$. The debt guarantor pays the share $\theta$ of offtaker losses that reaches lenders and recovers $\tilde R_D$ of it, plus the expected cost $\psi$ of other events; on acceleration it pays the outstanding principal. (iii) Dividing the loss removed by the expected cost gives @eq-efficiency, using $h = \varphi(m\lambda)(1-\tilde R)$. The contract guarantee is at least as efficient iff $h/c_C \ge \theta h/c_D$, that is iff $\theta\varphi(\lambda)(1 - \tilde R_D) + \psi \ge \theta\varphi(\lambda)(1 - \tilde R_G)$, which holds whenever $\tilde R_G \ge \tilde R_D$ because $\psi \ge 0$. Finally $h/c_C \ge 1$ iff $\varphi(m\lambda)(1 - \tilde R) \ge \varphi(\lambda)(1 - \tilde R_G)$, which holds when $m \ge 1$ (so $\varphi(m\lambda) \ge \varphi(\lambda)$) and $\tilde R_G \ge \tilde R$.

*Proposition 3.* (i) The expected unrecovered shortfall per year is $\varphi(\lambda)A(1 - \tilde R)$. It reaches layer $k$ only if each layer $j < k$ fails to pay, which happens with probability $\prod_{j<k}(1-q_j)$ by independence, and layer $k$ then pays with probability $q_k$. The facility bears what no layer pays. If $q_K = 1$ the product $\prod_{k \le K}(1 - q_k)$ is zero. (ii) In the one-factor model, offtaker $i$ enters an episode within the year if $\sqrt{\rho}Z + \sqrt{1-\rho}\varepsilon_i < \Phi^{-1}(p)$, with $Z$ and $\varepsilon_i$ independent standard normal. As $M \to \infty$, the share in episodes conditional on $Z$ converges to $\Phi\big((\Phi^{-1}(p) - \sqrt{\rho}Z)/\sqrt{1-\rho}\big)$, which is decreasing in $Z$, so its $1 - \varepsilon$ quantile is obtained at $Z = -\Phi^{-1}(1-\varepsilon)$ [@Vasicek2002]. With equal contract sizes the facility must fund this share of payments for $H$ years before the sovereign layer pays, which gives @eq-buffer. If $B$ meets the bound and the last layer's committed capacity covers the shortfall reaching it at the same quantile, generators are paid in full in all but an $\varepsilon$ share of years, and losses fall only on the layers.
